name: Phenol-croton oil peel
lead: The phenol-croton oil peel is a deep chemical peel that physicians use to smooth wrinkles, tighten loose skin and refresh sun-damaged facial skin. A controlled chemical injury removes the outer layers and stimulates the deeper dermis to rebuild, and as the skin heals the surface looks smoother and firmer. The classic Baker-Gordon formula, published in 1962, was long considered the standard for deep facial resurfacing.[1][3]

Reviews report that classical high-phenol formulas have largely been replaced by formulas with lower phenol and croton oil concentrations, which are described as having a better safety profile and more natural results, without the complete pigment loss once typical of deep peels.[1] Plastic surgeon Gregory Hetter argued in a 2000 series of papers that croton oil, rather than phenol, is the peel's active ingredient, and that peel depth can be customised by changing the croton oil concentration.[1][3][4]

The procedure is performed by physicians, often under sedation, and recovery is longer than for light or medium peels. Published research includes surgeon-authored formula studies, a retrospective outcomes review of peels combined with facelift surgery, and laboratory work on how the peel stimulates collagen.[8][9]

paras: Phenol-croton oil peels are applied by a physician and cause a controlled deep injury to the skin. In the medical literature the term phenol-croton oil peel has replaced the older phrase phenol peel, reflecting the view that croton oil supplies the caustic exfoliating action.[2] Wikipedia notes that early versions were very painful and often used general anesthesia, whereas newer formulations can be used under oral or intravenous sedation with local anesthetic injections.[2]

A typical review describes chemical peeling as a four-step process: preparation of the skin, the peel itself, a recovery phase and a maintenance phase. Peels are classed as superficial, medium or deep, and can be combined or applied in a mosaic pattern across different facial zones; deep peels need rigorous training and a learning curve, according to the French review.[14]

Hetter's refinements include customising the croton oil strength for delicate areas such as the eyelids and the neck.[13] Neck skin rejuvenation has been the subject of its own review in this field.[16]

A series of 2000 papers in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery dissected the classic formula. Part I examined which ingredients are active and tested the beliefs handed down since 1960 that phenol is the active agent, that phenol peels more deeply at lower concentrations, and that other additives matter; the author reported that phenol alone below 50% had no significant peeling effect without taping, and that croton oil drove peeling depth.[3] Part IV presented peeling solutions using phenol between 16% and 50% as a carrier for croton oil, with a topographic map of the face dividing it into regions that receive different strengths.[5]

Parts II and III looked at the history. The lay peelers who worked outside medicine recognised croton oil as a critical ingredient, while physicians who took up face peeling in the mid-1950s focused on phenol and did not initially appreciate the intense cytotoxic effect of croton resin.[6][7] A later paper described an animal model for scientific investigation of the peel.[10] A 2024 exchange in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology between formula authors discusses whether emulsifiers are needed to make deep peel formulas.[17]

Deep peels work by wounding the epidermis and upper dermis and prompting the skin to regenerate. A 2022 laboratory letter reported that the peel increased type 1 and type 3 collagen amounts through stimulation of SIRT-6 and SIRT-7.[9] Another 2022 letter reported that the new collagen formation after the peel occurs independently of the MMP-1, MMP-2, JunB and p53 pathways.[15] These are laboratory findings on skin tissue, not trials of cosmetic outcome.

A retrospective review of 47 consecutive patients who had a facelift combined with a perioral phenol-croton oil peel assessed outcomes using a validated patient satisfaction questionnaire and other objective measures, and reported significant central face skin tightening and wrinkle reduction; the authors describe the combination as an underappreciated tool for face rejuvenation.[8]

A small registered trial (NCT02848209, 9 participants) compared the histology of different peeling agents in surgically undermined skin.[11] The Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology continuing-education review summarises the historical, scientific and procedural literature and concludes that modern lower-concentration formulas have improved the safety profile of deep peels.[1] A review of chemical peeling more broadly covers rejuvenation, actinic damage and dyschromias across depths.[12]

Wikipedia notes that the deeper the peel, the more complications can arise, with reported issues including photosensitivity, prolonged redness, pigmentary changes, milia, skin atrophy and textural change.[2] The 2019 review notes that a deep peel no longer has to mean the complete facial depigmentation, the so-called alabaster look, associated with the older high-phenol formulas.[1] Pre-peel assessment of depth of damage, contraindications and patient-specific limits is described as part of the standard approach.[14]

Austrian dermatologist Ferdinand von Hebra (1816-1880) used phenol, croton oil and nitric acid on the skin in the second half of the 19th century.[2] According to Wikipedia, phenol-croton oil peels were used covertly by early Hollywood stars in the 1920s before Thomas Baker and Howard Gordon brought the procedure into mainstream practice in the 1960s.[2] Baker published his simple formula in 1962, and it became the version used by most plastic surgeons and dermatologists for decades.[3] In 2000 Hetter's series reframed the formula around croton oil.[3][5]

card.summary: The classic deep surgical-grade peel for wrinkles and tightening, now used in gentler low-phenol versions.
card.note: Deep peel done by physicians; pigment loss, scarring and prolonged recovery are documented.

quick.overview:
A phenol-croton oil peel is a deep chemical peel used for wrinkles and skin tightening. The classic 1962 Baker-Gordon formula has largely been replaced by lower-concentration versions.

Evidence is mostly surgeon case series, formula studies and lab work rather than randomized trials.
quick.mechanism: Croton oil is reported to be the main active peeling agent, with phenol acting as a carrier at lower concentrations; the peel injures the skin deeply and is followed by collagen remodeling.
quick.risks: Deeper peels carry more complications: prolonged redness, pigment change, atrophy and scarring. They are performed by physicians, often with sedation.

chain: Phenol and croton oil produce a controlled deep injury
Dermis remodels and lays down new collagen as it heals
Fewer wrinkles and tighter, smoother skin
angle.text: A deep peel is one of the strongest chemical options for fine to moderate wrinkles, perioral lines and skin laxity. Surgeons adjust the croton oil strength to match each facial area, and the peel is often paired with a facelift to treat the lower face and mouth region.
